step.text: Row 5 has only one empty cell, R5C8. The one digit it’s missing is 9.
The digit 4 is already placed 8 times (highlighted), so the 9th must go in R8C3.
Look at every 3 already placed (highlighted). Their rows and columns block 3 from all but one empty cell in box 7: R7C3.
R2C9 has only one candidate left: 4. Every other digit already appears in its row, column or box.
In row 3, the digit 2 fits in only one cell: R3C4. The cell may have other candidates, but 2 has nowhere else to go in this unit.
R2C1 and R8C1 both hold only {1,9}. Those two digits must fill those two cells, so 1 and 9 can be removed from the other cells in column 1 (struck through in red).
In row 1, the digits 6 and 9 fit only in R1C5 and R1C6. Those cells must hold 6 and 9, so every other candidate can be removed from them.
In box 3, 5 can only go in row 2 (R2C8, R2C9). So that box’s 5 is in this line, and 5 can be removed from the rest of the line.
In row 5, 4 can only go inside box 5 (R5C4, R5C6). So that box’s 4 is in this line, and 4 can be removed from the box’s other cells.
R2C3, R2C7, R2C8 in row 2 hold only the digits {1,2,5} between them. Those three digits must fill those three cells, so they can be removed from the other cells in row 2 (struck through in red).
In column 3, the digits 4, 6, 7 fit only in R4C3, R5C3, R6C3. Those three cells must hold those three digits, so every other candidate can be removed from them.

In two rows, the digit 8 has exactly two possible cells each (R7C3, R7C7, R9C3, R9C7), lined up in the same two columns. 8 must take one diagonal of this rectangle, so 8 can be removed from the rest of those two columns.

In three columns, the digit 6 has only two or three possible cells each (R1C3, R3C3, R1C7, R3C7, R9C7, R3C8, R9C8), all inside the same three rows. So 6 is used up inside those three rows, and can be removed from every other cell in them.

R7C2, R7C4, R7C5, R7C6 in row 7 hold only the digits {3,6,7,8} between them. Those four digits must fill those four cells, so they can be removed from the other cells in row 7 (struck through in red).
In box 9, the digits 1, 2, 3, 9 fit only in R7C9, R8C7, R8C9, R9C9. Those four cells must hold those four digits, so every other candidate can be removed from them.
Pivot R3C8 holds {5,7}. Wing R2C9 holds {7,9} and wing R3C3 holds {5,9}. Whichever way the pivot goes, one wing must be 9, so 9 can be removed from every cell that sees both wings.
Pivot R6C8 holds {3,5,6}. Wing R6C7 holds {3,6} and wing R6C9 holds {5,6}. Whatever the pivot becomes, 6 lands in the pivot or one wing, so 6 can be removed from every cell that sees all three.

In two columns, 2 has just two possible cells each (R3C7, R7C7, R2C9, R3C9). Two of them share a row, so at least one of the other two, R7C7 or R2C9, must be 2. Remove 2 from every cell that sees both.

R5C2 and R8C6 both hold only {7,8} and don't see each other. In row 7, 7 can only go in R7C2 or R7C5, which see R5C2 and R8C6. If neither were 8, both would be 7 and row 7 would have nowhere for its 7. So one of them is 8, and cells that see both can't be 8.

Join the places where 6 has only two options in a unit and colour them in turns: R7C1, R3C2 one colour, R7C2, R3C1 the other. One colour holds the 6s. R3C6 sees a cell of each colour, so it can't be 6.

In four columns, the digit 6 has only two to four possible cells each (R1C2, R2C2, R3C2, R1C5, R5C5, R1C6, R2C6, R3C6, R1C9, R2C9), all inside the same four rows. So 6 is used up inside those four rows, and can be removed from every other cell in them.

R7C2, R7C8, R8C8 hold only {1,9}, and R8C2 holds 1 and 9 plus more. The four cells sit in two rows, two columns and two boxes. If R8C2 were 1 or 9, the 1s and 9s could swap and the puzzle would have two solutions. It has one, so remove 1 and 9 from R8C2.

Every empty cell has exactly two candidates except R2C9, which has three. Each digit appears twice in every row, column and box, except 7, which appears three times around R2C9. Without that extra 7 the grid would have two solutions, so R2C9 must be 7.
